sps, also known as stiff -man syndrome) is a rare, potentially debilitating disease of uncertain etiology presenting with variable psychiatric and somatic symptoms that often leave the af ﬂicted with no solid medical diagnosis and poorly controlled symptoms.1–5 sps was ﬁrst described by moersch and woltman, who over 30 years of practice categorized 14 of their patients in a case series reporting a constella- tion of symptoms such as ﬂuctuating muscular rigidity and spasticity.1 other reports with consistent ﬁndings were subsequently published in the same decade. 2 sps’s presentation is often associated with ﬂuctuating states of emotion, which frequently results in patients being treated for the syndrome as a purely psychiatric disorder. this can cause delays in diagnosis and management 3—in 1 reported case, the diagnosis of sps was made 18 years after symptom onset. 4 the hallmark clinical features of sps are muscular rigidity with episodic spastic spells in appendicular and truncal muscle groups, with a propensity to affect the para- spinal and lower-back muscles. patients may also exhibit autonomic instability in severe spells, including blood pressure ﬂuctuations, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and respiratory distress. 4 these spastic spells can be progressively debilitating and often have profound effects on mobility and overall quality of life. environ- mental or emotional stimuli are often triggers, further complicating the diagnosis and often resulting in erroneous diagnoses, including panic disorder, con- version disorder, and even anorexia nervosa. 3,5–7 more recently, literature has suggested that certain medications, such as serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, might also be precipitants of these spells. 8 case report mrs. a, a 32-year-old woman with an extensive history of psychiatric conditions (including panic disorder, depression, anxiety) and a remote diagnosis of seizure disorder presented to the emergency department (ed) with shock and hyperthermia after being started on buspirone. she would be hospitalized in the intensive care unit for nearly a month. prior to her presentation, for the 10 preceding years, she had frequent “panic report of her husband, these events were typically managed with benzodiazepines both at home and in the ed. these spastic spells would be triggered by sudden stimuli, regardless of their intensity, and got progressively more frequent and dramatic. her hus- band reported that his coughing or sneezing could precipitate a spell where she would be unable to ambulate on her own for anywhere from 15 anxiety disorders and her somatic symptoms were eventually designated largely as somatization. her husband reported that she had found the most signi ﬁcant relief of her symptoms (both psychiatric and somatic) while on an unknown dose of clonazepam and duloxetine a few years prior, but that a medical decision was made to wean her off these agents. she had intermittent and inconsistent follow-up with psychiatrists over the following years. before her presentation, she was on gabapentin 800 mg 3 times a day, acetaminophen-hydrocodone 5–325 mg 1 –2 times daily, tizanidine 4 mg 3 times a day,
